content: An herbalist is an individual who dedicates their life to understanding and utilizing plants for economic or medicinal purposes. They possess expertise in the harvesting and collection of medicinal plants, a practice often referred to as wildcrafting. In specific traditions, such as Traditional Chinese Medicine, an herbalist is trained or skilled in preparing and dispensing herbal prescriptions, functioning as a traditional Chinese herb doctor. Similarly, in the Ayurvedic tradition, an Ayurvedic herbalist is trained in the preparation and administration of herbal remedies according to Ayurvedic principles. Herbalists are professionals who specialize in the therapeutic application of medicinal plants. Their practice, known as herbalism, involves the use of herbs—also referred to as botanical or crude medicine—to address health concerns and promote well-being. Professional designations for herbalists vary and include titles such as: Registered Herbalist (RH) from the American Herbalists Guild (AHG), Diplomate in Oriental Medicine (NCCAOM) from the National Certification Commission for Acupuncture and Oriental Medicine, Full Member of the National Herbalists Association of Australia (MNHAA), Fellow of the National Herbalists Association of Australia (FNHAA), which is awarded to Full Members with at least 10 years of membership, clinical practice, and significant contributions to the profession or association, Member of the National Institute of Medical Herbalists (MNIMH) in the UK, or Member of The Irish Institute of Medical Herbalists (MIIMH). The education and training of herbalists vary significantly across the globe. In many cases, lay herbalists and practitioners of traditional indigenous medicine acquire their knowledge through apprenticeships and recognition within their communities, rather than through formal education. In some countries, however, formalized training programs and minimum educational standards exist, though these standards are not always consistent within or between nations. For instance, in Australia, the profession is self-regulated, leading to different associations establishing varying educational requirements. Educational qualifications for herbalists in Australia range from Diplomas to Master’s degrees, with Advanced Diplomas being partially regulated by the national Health Training Packages issued by the Australian National Training Authority. The Course Accreditation System Version 2, developed by the National Herbalists Association of Australia, is widely regarded as the most rigorous and professional standard in the country. Herbalists may engage in the cultivation or wildcrafting of herbs, as well as in the diagnosis and treatment of health conditions. They often dispense herbal medications tailored to the needs of their clients. Most herbal traditions emphasize a constitutional analysis of the individual, focusing on treating the patient as a whole rather than merely addressing the disease.
